title: Redis vs Valkey for a platform team
topic: Research Redis vs Valkey for a platform team choosing an in-memory data store: licensing, governance, architecture, persistence, clustering, performance, compatibility and migration, as of late 2026. Use public sources, primary documentation first. Save a cited report.
scope: Redis (Redis Ltd.'s open-source Redis / Redis Open Source) and Valkey (the Linux Foundation fork) as in-memory data stores, as of late 2026, for a platform team choosing between them: licensing, governance and project history, architecture, persistence, clustering and replication, published performance claims, compatibility, and migration. Primary documentation, licence texts and project announcements first. Out of scope: managed-service pricing, client-library comparisons, and vendor enterprise editions beyond what bears on licensing.
prose_review: not independently reviewed at light depth

questions.question: Under which licences is current Redis released, and how have they changed since 2024?
questions.subject: redis

headline.sentence: Redis Open Source 8 and later is offered under a choice of RSALv2, SSPLv1 or AGPLv3, following a March 2024 change that moved Redis from the BSD licence to dual RSALv2/SSPLv1 starting with Redis 7.4.

answer.sentence: In March 2024 Redis Ltd. announced that, starting with Redis 7.4, Redis would be dual-licensed under RSALv2 and SSPLv1 and no longer distributed under the three-clause BSD licence.
Redis Ltd. said at the time that organizations providing competitive offerings could not use new Redis versions free of charge under those terms, while non-competing users were unaffected.
Redis Open Source 8 and later versions let users choose among RSALv2, SSPLv1 and AGPLv3.
Redis Ltd. states that RSALv2 and SSPLv1 are not open source licences, whereas AGPLv3, added with Redis 8, is OSI-approved.
Redis 8 also folds RediSearch, RedisJSON, RedisTimeSeries and RedisBloom into Redis Open Source under the same tri-licence as core Redis.
Earlier releases keep their original terms: Redis 7.2.x and earlier remain under the BSD3 licence, and Redis Community Edition 7.4.x to 7.8.x remain under the dual RSALv2/SSPLv1 licence.

questions.question: Under which licence is Valkey released?
questions.subject: valkey

headline.sentence: Valkey is released under the BSD 3-Clause licence, per its repository COPYING file.

answer.sentence: Valkey's repository COPYING file gives the BSD 3-Clause licence.
That file carries both a 2024-present copyright notice for Valkey contributors and a 2006-2020 copyright notice for Redis Ltd.
According to the Valkey README and the Linux Foundation launch announcement, Valkey was forked from open source Redis 7.2.4, just before Redis moved to source-available licences.

Redis 7.2.x and earlier remain under the BSD3 licence, so Valkey continues the licence of the Redis line it was forked from, while Redis Open Source 8 and later instead offers a choice of RSALv2, SSPLv1 and AGPLv3.
At Valkey's launch, the Linux Foundation's CTO said foundation stewardship means Valkey will be community-driven without surprise licence changes, a commitment made by the project's own steward.

questions.question: Who owns and governs the Redis project?
questions.subject: redis

headline.sentence: Redis is owned and steered by the company Redis Ltd., which holds the Redis trademarks, requires a contributor licence agreement for code contributions and describes itself as the code's maintainer.

answer.sentence: Redis the company is the registered owner of the Redis name and logo and sets the requirements for using those trademarks.
Redis accepts code contributions only under the Redis Software Grant and Contributor License Agreement that Redis Ltd. requires.
When announcing its licence change, Redis Inc. described itself as the maintainer of the Redis code and said it sponsored the bulk of Redis development alongside a community of contributors.
Redis Inc. framed that licence change as its own decision, made despite efforts to support a community-led governance model and a desire to keep the BSD license.

Later licensing direction also came from the company: Redis CEO Rowan Trollope announced AGPL as an added licensing option starting with Redis 8, with guidance from Salvatore, CTO Benjamin Renaud and core developers.
These descriptions of Redis's governance come from Redis's own announcements and pages rather than independent sources.
By contrast, Valkey is governed by a Technical Steering Committee of its repository maintainers and committed to open governance at the Linux Foundation.

questions.question: Who governs Valkey, and under which foundation?
questions.subject: valkey

headline.sentence: Valkey is governed by a Technical Steering Committee of its maintainers, chaired by Madelyn Olson, under open governance at the Linux Foundation.

answer.sentence: The Linux Foundation announced on March 28, 2024 its intent to form Valkey as an open source alternative to Redis.
At launch, Valkey was backed by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson and Snap Inc. and committed to open governance at the Linux Foundation.
The Linux Foundation's CTO said foundation stewardship means Valkey will be community-driven without surprise licence changes.
A Technical Steering Committee made up of the maintainers of the Valkey repository oversees all technical, project, approval and policy matters.

No single organization may hold more than one third of TSC seats, and major decisions, such as changing the governance document or adding TSC members, need a two-thirds supermajority of the entire TSC.
Madelyn Olson chairs the TSC, and its maintainers come from several companies including Amazon, Google, Oracle, Ericsson, Tencent, Apple, Alibaba and Percona.
This differs from Redis, where the company Redis Ltd. owns the trademarks and requires its own contributor licence agreement for code contributions.

questions.question: Why and from which Redis version was Valkey forked?

headline.sentence: Valkey was forked from open source Redis 7.2.4 in response to Redis's move away from the BSD licence starting with Redis 7.4.

answer.sentence: Redis announced that, starting with Redis 7.4, it would be dual-licensed under RSALv2 and SSPLv1 and no longer distributed under the BSD 3-clause license.
Redis Ltd. states that RSALv2 and SSPLv1 are not open source licences, while Redis 7.2.x and earlier remain under the BSD3 licence.
According to the Linux Foundation's March 28, 2024 launch announcement, Valkey was formed in response to that licence change and continued development from Redis 7.2.4 under the BSD 3-clause license.
The Valkey README likewise states that Valkey was forked from open source Redis right before Redis moved to source-available licenses.
Valkey co-creator Madelyn Olson, a Redis core team member until Redis 7.2, said Valkey lets contributors continue where they left off in open source.
Redis's own later account agrees on the cause: Redis CEO Rowan Trollope wrote that the March 2024 move to SSPL led AWS and Google to maintain their own fork but hurt Redis's community relationship.
In the same announcement, Redis added AGPL as a licensing option starting with Redis 8.
These accounts come from the parties involved, the Linux Foundation and Valkey on one side and Redis's CEO on the other, rather than from independent sources.

questions.question: How does Redis use threads to process commands and network I/O?
questions.subject: redis

headline.sentence: Redis runs all command execution on a single main thread, uses side threads for slow I/O and operations such as UNLINK, and can optionally move client socket reads, writes and parsing to I/O threads, which are disabled by default.

answer.sentence: Redis describes its design as mostly single-threaded: one thread serves all client requests through multiplexing, and since Redis 2.4 background threads have handled mainly slow disk I/O.
Certain operations such as UNLINK and slow I/O also run on side threads.
Redis introduced I/O threads in 6.0, and in that implementation the main thread was blocked while I/O threads read and wrote, waiting for all of them to complete their current tasks.
Redis 8.0 introduced a new I/O threading implementation that always uses threads for both reads and writes, so the io-threads-do-reads setting is no longer effective.
In Redis's asynchronous I/O threads design, all command execution stays on the main thread, while each I/O thread runs its own event loop handling client reads and writes.
I/O threading is off by default (io-threads 1), and Redis recommends enabling it only on machines with at least 4 cores while leaving a spare core, for example 3 I/O threads on four cores.
Throughput figures for the Redis 8 threading come from Redis Ltd.'s own measurements and are covered in the Performance section.

questions.question: How does Valkey use threads to process commands and network I/O?
questions.subject: valkey

headline.sentence: Valkey keeps command execution single-threaded, runs some operations on side threads, and can optionally hand reading, parsing, writing, polling and memory deallocation to I/O threads, which are disabled by default.

answer.sentence: Valkey's configuration describes the server as mostly single-threaded, with certain operations such as UNLINK and slow I/O accesses performed on side threads.
Command execution stays single-threaded, and the Valkey 8 I/O threads are worker threads that take jobs from the main thread such as reading, parsing, writing, polling and memory deallocation.

The design described on the Valkey blog has the main thread orchestrate I/O thread jobs, adjust the number of active I/O threads to current load, and keep client-to-thread affinity for memory locality.
In that design, epoll_wait, which consumed more than 20 percent of the time when run solely by the main thread, is offloaded to I/O threads one thread at a time.
Before executing commands, the main thread also runs a prefetch-commands-keys procedure to reduce external memory accesses on the main dictionary.
These details are the Valkey project's own description of its Valkey 8 I/O threading, not an independent account.
The Valkey project reports that Valkey 8.1 offloads TLS negotiation and other TLS-handling calls to I/O threads, and says Valkey 9.1.0 has a new IO threading model that adds up to 17% throughput.

Valkey's current configuration disables I/O threading by default and suggests enabling it only with at least 3 cores; when enabled, I/O threads handle reads and writes, and io-threads-do-reads is deprecated with no effect.

Both projects keep command execution on the main thread and disable I/O threading by default, with Redis recommending at least 4 cores and Valkey suggesting at least 3, and both have made io-threads-do-reads ineffective.

questions.question: Which persistence options does Redis document?
questions.subject: redis

headline.sentence: Redis documents these persistence options: RDB point-in-time snapshots, AOF logging of every write, no persistence, and RDB plus AOF combined in the same instance.

answer.sentence: According to its own documentation, Redis offers RDB point-in-time snapshots, AOF logging of every write, no persistence, or both RDB and AOF together in one instance.
RDB snapshots are saved to dump.rdb by default, and a setting such as save 60 1000 snapshots every 60 seconds if at least 1000 keys changed.
AOF offers the fsync policies always, everysec and no, and the documentation says that with everysec Redis may lose 1 second of data in a disaster.
Since Redis 7.0.0, the AOF is multi-part: at most one base file plus incremental files, tracked by a manifest in a separate directory.
When both AOF and RDB are enabled, Redis rebuilds the dataset from the AOF on restart because it is the most complete.
Redis also documents a BACKUP command family, available since Redis 8.10.0, that produces a restorable backup without stopping writes by reusing the multi-part AOF format.
The Valkey persistence facts in this report record no equivalent BACKUP command family.

questions.question: Which persistence options does Valkey document?
questions.subject: valkey

headline.sentence: Valkey documents the same persistence options as Redis: RDB snapshots, AOF logging, no persistence, and RDB plus AOF combined.

answer.sentence: Valkey's own documentation lists RDB point-in-time snapshots, AOF logging of every write, no persistence, and combined RDB plus AOF in the same instance, matching the options Redis documents.
RDB snapshotting is enabled by default, snapshots go to dump.rdb, and a setting such as save 60 1000 snapshots every 60 seconds if at least 1000 keys changed.
For uses such as a pure cache, Valkey documents disabling persistence by setting the save parameter to an empty string.
Valkey's AOF offers the same fsync policies as Redis (always, everysec and no), and with everysec Valkey may lose 1 second of data in a disaster.

Valkey also uses a multi-part AOF of at most one base file plus incremental files tracked by a manifest file in a separate directory, and rebuilds from the AOF on restart when both AOF and RDB are enabled.
The documented options look alike, but Valkey cannot use data files produced by Redis Community Edition 7.4 and later, including RDB files.
Redis Community Edition 7.4 release notes record RDB file format changes for per-field hash expiration.

questions.question: How does Redis Cluster shard data and handle replication and failover?
questions.subject: redis

headline.sentence: Redis Cluster shards keys across 16384 hash slots, replicates asynchronously, and fails over by electing a replica with ACKs from a majority of masters.

answer.sentence: Redis Cluster computes each key's slot as the CRC16 of the key modulo 16384, and every node is responsible for a subset of those slots.
Its stated target is linear scalability up to 1000 nodes without proxies, which is lower than the 2000-node design goal Valkey states for its cluster.
Redis 8.4.0 added the CLUSTER MIGRATION command, which provides atomic slot migration; Valkey added a comparable atomic slot migration in 9.0 under a different command name, CLUSTER MIGRATESLOTS.

Replication in Redis Cluster is asynchronous with a last-failover-wins merge, so writes can be lost during partitions, and nodes do not wait for write acknowledgments unless a client explicitly requests them with WAIT.

A node is marked FAIL when a majority of masters confirm it is failing, and the majority side of a partition recovers after NODE_TIMEOUT plus a few seconds, with failovers usually taking 1 or 2 seconds.
A replica wins the failover election once it receives ACKs from a majority of masters, then obtains a new configEpoch higher than that of any other existing master.
Valkey documents the same majority-ACK election and the same recovery timing, which matches the shared design of the two cluster implementations described in these facts.

questions.question: How does Valkey cluster mode shard data and handle replication and failover?
questions.subject: valkey

headline.sentence: Valkey cluster mode shards keys across 16384 hash slots, replicates asynchronously, and fails over by electing a replica with ACKs from a majority of primaries.

answer.sentence: Valkey Cluster assigns each key to one of 16384 hash slots by CRC16(key) mod 16384, with each primary handling a subset, the same slot scheme Redis Cluster uses.

Its stated design goal is linear scalability up to 2000 nodes with no proxies, against the 1000-node target stated for Redis Cluster; these are the projects' own stated goals rather than measured results.
The Valkey project also claims that Valkey 9.0 scales clusters to 2,000 nodes.
Replication is asynchronous with a last-failover-wins merge, so writes can be lost during partitions, the same limitation documented for Redis Cluster.

A replica wins the failover election once it receives ACKs from the majority of primaries, and the majority side recovers after NODE_TIMEOUT plus a few seconds, with failovers usually taking 1 or 2 seconds.

Valkey 9.0 introduced atomic slot migration, started with CLUSTER MIGRATESLOTS, as the recommended live-resharding method, which the project describes as faster and more reliable than legacy slot migration.
From version 9.0, Valkey cluster mode also supports multiple databases through the cluster-databases setting, which defaults to 1.

questions.question: What performance improvements do recent Redis releases claim?
questions.subject: redis

headline.sentence: Redis Ltd. claims Redis 8 brings over 30 performance improvements and makes further throughput and memory claims for Redis 8.2 and 8.4, all from its own benchmarks against earlier Redis releases.

answer.sentence: Redis Ltd. claims Redis 8 has over 30 performance improvements, including up to 87% faster commands, up to 2x more operations per second throughput and up to 18% faster replication.
In its own benchmark of 149 tests against Redis 7.2.5, Redis Ltd. reports that 90 commands ran faster in Redis 8, with p50 latency reductions from 5.4% to 87.4%.

Redis 8 introduces a new I/O threading implementation that is off by default (io-threads 1), and Redis Ltd. measured up to 112% higher throughput with 8 threads on a multi-core Intel CPU, varying by command.
Redis Ltd. reports that Redis 8's new replication mechanism, in a 10 GB full-sync test, cut replication time 18%, lowered the peak primary replication buffer 35% and allowed a 7.5% higher write rate.
For Redis 8.2, Redis Ltd. claims up to 49% more throughput than Redis 8.0 with 8 I/O threads on a 20% write, 80% read caching workload, exceeding 1 million operations per second per instance.
The Redis 8.4 GA release notes claim I/O threading throughput gains above 30% for caching use cases (10% SET, 90% GET) on 4 cores, and up to 91% JSON memory reduction for homogeneous arrays.
Every figure here is Redis Ltd.'s own claim, measured by Redis Ltd. against its own earlier Redis releases under conditions it chose.

questions.question: What performance improvements do recent Valkey releases claim?
questions.subject: valkey

headline.sentence: The Valkey project and its contributors claim throughput, memory and command-speed gains across Valkey 8, 8.1, 9.0 and 9.1.0, measured against earlier Valkey releases or under their own test conditions.

answer.sentence: Valkey project blog authors from AWS report that Valkey 8's new I/O threading, together with a prefetch change, raised SET throughput about 230%, from 360K to 1.19M requests per second versus Valkey 7.2, with 8 I/O threads on C7g.16xlarge.
The Valkey project says Valkey 8.1's rewritten hashtable saves roughly 20 bytes per key (up to 30 with TTL) and improves throughput about 10% over 8.0 for pipelined workloads without I/O threading.
The project also claims Valkey 8.1 makes ZRANK up to 45% faster, HyperLogLog PFMERGE/PFCOUNT 12x faster with x86 AVX, and BITCOUNT up to 514% faster using AVX2.

It reports that Valkey 8.1 offloads TLS negotiation to I/O threads, raising the new-connection accept rate around 300%, and that offloading other TLS-handling calls gave observed 10% SET and 22% GET throughput gains.

For Valkey 9.0, the project claims clusters scale to 2,000 nodes and over 1 billion requests per second, with pipeline memory prefetch giving up to 40%, and zero-copy for large requests up to 20%, higher throughput.

The project says Valkey 9.1.0 reaches 2.1 million requests per second on a single server (512-byte payloads, 9 IO threads, pipeline depth 10), and that its new IO threading model adds up to 17% throughput.
Every figure here is a claim by the Valkey project or its blog authors, measured against earlier Valkey releases or on hardware and settings they chose.

questions.question: Which data types and features does Redis offer that Valkey does not document?
questions.subject: redis

headline.sentence: Redis documents time series, vector sets, arrays and probabilistic types such as count-min sketch, cuckoo filter, t-digest and Top-K that Valkey's data types page does not list, while JSON and similarity search have Valkey module counterparts.

answer.sentence: As of May 2025, Redis 8 added 8 more data structures to Redis Open Source, including vector set in beta, JSON, time series, and five probabilistic structures such as cuckoo filter, count-min sketch, top-k and t-digest.
Redis Ltd. also merged Redis Stack into a single Redis Open Source distribution that includes all the former modules.
Redis Open Source's data types page documents time series, arrays, count-min sketch and t-digest types.
It also documents vector sets, an HNSW-based type for vector similarity search using cosine similarity, launched in beta with an API that may change.
Valkey's data types page documents HyperLogLog and Bloom filters, the latter through the valkey-bloom module, but not count-min sketch, cuckoo filter, t-digest or Top-K.
JSON storage with JSONPath and index-based similarity search are not Redis-only, because Valkey Bundle documents a Valkey JSON module and a Valkey Search module for them.
Not every recent Redis feature is missing from Valkey: Valkey 9.0 introduced hash field expiration, which Redis 7.4 had added.
The absences on the Valkey side come from what its data types page lists, not from a Valkey statement of which Redis types it lacks.

questions.question: How compatible is Valkey with Redis commands, protocol and data files?
questions.subject: valkey

headline.sentence: Valkey is compatible with Redis OSS 7.2 and earlier in commands, configuration, protocol and modules, but cannot use data files from Redis Community Edition 7.4 and later.

answer.sentence: Valkey 7.2.4 is a fork of Redis OSS 7.2.4, which makes Valkey compatible with Redis OSS 7.2 and all earlier open-source Redis versions.

Valkey's migration guide states that Valkey uses the RESP wire protocol with RESP2 and RESP3 support, that existing Redis client libraries connect to Valkey without code changes, and that redis-cli works with Valkey servers.
Valkey accepts Redis-style configuration files and supports existing Redis OSS 7.2 configuration directives.

It reports redis_version:7.2.4 in INFO for backward compatibility and keeps Lua scripts using the redis namespace working, and the guide says to use server_name and valkey_version to detect the actual Valkey server and version.
Modules written for Redis OSS run on Valkey against the RedisModule_ API, and Valkey adds its own ValkeyModule_ API for new modules.
Data files are the break point: Valkey cannot use data files produced by Redis Community Edition 7.4 and later, including RDB files.
Redis Community Edition 7.4 release notes record RDB file format changes for per-field hash expiration.
These compatibility statements come from Valkey's own migration guide.

questions.question: What migration path from Redis to Valkey does the Valkey project document?

headline.sentence: Valkey's migration guide documents physical migration of a Redis RDB snapshot, a replication-based cutover for standalone servers, and a replica-promotion procedure for Redis Cluster, treating migration from Redis OSS 7.2 and earlier as effectively an upgrade.

answer.sentence: The guide states that Valkey is compatible with Redis OSS 7.2 and earlier because Valkey 7.2.4 forked Redis OSS 7.2.4, so such migrations are effectively an upgrade.
For a standalone Redis server, the guide lists physical migration, which copies the most recent on-disk snapshot from Redis to Valkey, among its options.
It calls physical migration the easiest and fastest method, at the cost of downtime while Valkey loads the data.
To minimise downtime, the guide instead configures Valkey as a replica of Redis and later stops replication on Valkey with REPLICAOF NO ONE.
For Redis Cluster, the guide adds Valkey nodes as replicas, promotes one Valkey replica to primary for each Redis primary, and then removes the Redis nodes.
The guide also covers migrating only a specific set of critical keys, and it names RIOT, RedisShake and Redis-Migrate-Tool as data migration tools that are beyond its scope.

questions.question: Which Redis versions or features limit a straightforward migration to Valkey?

headline.sentence: Valkey's guide says data files from Redis Community Edition 7.4 and later are not compatible with Valkey, and that proprietary Redis versions need a method it does not cover; which later features cause this is only partly documented.

answer.sentence: The Valkey migration guide states that Redis Community Edition 7.4 and later produce data files that are not compatible with Valkey.
The Redis Community Edition 7.4 release notes record RDB file format changes for per-field hash expiration and also note a licence change.
The guide says migrating from proprietary Redis versions and other Redis-like software may be possible but needs another method that it does not cover.
For physical migration, the guide warns that having AOF enabled on Valkey's first start prevents the copied Redis RDB file from being imported.
It also warns of possible data loss with physical migration on write-heavy instances, and with replication cutover if writes continue while Redis syncs to the Valkey replica.
Valkey reports redis_version:7.2.4 in INFO for backward compatibility, and the guide says to use server_name and valkey_version to detect the actual Valkey server and version.
The guide does not say which features of Redis Community Edition 7.4 and later cause the incompatibility, and it documents no method for migrating from those versions.

questions.question: Which commands added in Redis 7.4 and 8.x does Valkey implement or lack?
questions.subject: valkey

headline.sentence: Valkey implements Redis 7.4's hash field expiration from Valkey 9.0, Redis 8.0's HSETEX and HGETEX in Valkey 9.0, and Redis 8.0's HGETDEL in Valkey 9.1.

answer.sentence: Valkey 9.0 introduced hash field expiration, covering commands such as HPERSIST, HTTL and HEXPIRETIME that Redis 7.4 added among nine per-field expiration commands.
RedisShake's compatibility page lists hash field expiration as unsupported on Valkey 8.x.
Valkey 9.0 includes the HSETEX and HGETEX hash commands that Redis 8.0 added, as Valkey 9.0 patch notes fix HSETEX notifications and HGETEX permissions.
Valkey 9.1 added HGETDEL, which Redis 8.0 introduced to get and delete the value of one or more hash fields.
Valkey 9.1 also added an MSETEX command that sets multiple keys with a shared expiration.
Redis 8 brought vector set in beta, JSON, time series and probabilistic structures into Redis Open Source, while Valkey Bundle documents separate Valkey JSON and Valkey Search modules.

questions.question: What independent, third-party benchmarks compare recent Redis and Valkey releases?

headline.sentence: The cross-project benchmarks cited come from Momento, a cache vendor, which reported Valkey ahead of Redis on throughput, latency and memory in its own tests.

answer.sentence: Momento, a cache vendor, reported Valkey 8.1.1 at 999.8K SET RPS with .8ms p99 and Redis 8.0 at a printed 729.4 RPS, with no K suffix, and .99ms p99, on a tuned 8-vCPU c8g.2xl with 1KB items.
In that Momento test, Valkey 8.1 had 37% higher SET and 16% higher GET throughput than Redis 8.0, with 30% faster SET p99 and 60%+ faster GET p99.
Momento also reported that I/O threading lifted Valkey SET throughput from 239K to 678K RPS and Redis from 235K to 563K RPS, moving from no I/O threads to 6 threads.

Momento separately measured Valkey 8.1.1 using 3.77 GB versus Redis 8.2 using 4.83 GB (28% less) after 50 million sorted-set inserts on an 8-vCPU c8g.2xl, with Valkey finishing at about 570k inserts per second versus about 530k.
These figures are Momento's own measurements on an 8-vCPU c8g.2xl that it tuned, not claims made by either project.

questions.question: Which tools or managed services support migrating data from Redis 7.4 or later to Valkey?

headline.sentence: RedisShake supports Redis up to 8.4.x and Valkey 8.x to 9.x, and ElastiCache documents a managed Redis OSS to Valkey upgrade, but Valkey's guide says Redis Community Edition 7.4 and later data files are incompatible.

answer.sentence: Valkey's migration guide says Redis Community Edition 7.4 and later produce data files that are not compatible with Valkey, and it names RIOT, RedisShake and Redis-Migrate-Tool as data migration tools while treating them as beyond its scope.
The RedisShake README says it supports Redis 2.8 to 8.4.x and Valkey 8.x to 9.x, with PSync, RDB and Scan data fetch methods.
Its compatibility page lists Vector Sets and Redis Stack modules as not supported for Redis 8.x, and hash field expiration as unsupported on Valkey 8.x.
The README also says RedisShake 4.x does not support resumable transfer and that RedisShake is best suited for one-time data migration rather than long-term continuous synchronization.
RIOT's README says RIOT, which supports Redis with live and/or snapshot replication, has been superseded by RIOT-X, an enterprise-grade version actively supported by Redis, Inc..

Amazon ElastiCache documents upgrading from Redis OSS to Valkey through the Console, API or CLI by specifying the new engine and major engine version, and describes Valkey as designed as a drop-in replacement for Redis OSS 7.
None of these sources explicitly documents migrating data from Redis Community Edition 7.4 or later into Valkey.

citations.quote: We spun up an AWS c8g.2xl (Graviton4) instance with 8 vCPUs and 16 GB RAM. We ran Valkey 8.1.1 and Redis 8.2 on the same node. Using an in-house benchmarking harness written in Rust, we inserted 50 million items into a sorted set, 250k at a time, and recorded used memory (INFO MEMORY), throughput, and ZSET size after each million inserts.

From the start, Valkey was more frugal. At 1 M inserts, Valkey used ~80 MB of memory while Redis used ~100 MB. By the time we reached 50 M entries, Valkey consumed 3.77 GB whereas Redis consumed 4.83 GB, a difference of 1.06 GB (28 %). That reduction aligns with Valkey’s per‑key overhead savings and the Linux Foundation’s claim that upgrading to Valkey 8.1 can reduce memory footprints by up to 20 % for most workloads. Throughput told a similar story: Redis initially led, but Valkey held steady and finished the run at ~570 k inserts/s while Redis dropped to ~530 k/s, a ~7 % difference.

gaps.question: redis-performance

gaps.question: valkey-performance

gaps.question: independent-benchmarks
gaps.reason: Checker's assessment: the only benchmarks cited are from Momento, which is not part of either project. No benchmark from an analyst, academic, the press or another vendor is cited.

gaps.question: independent-benchmarks
gaps.reason: Checker's assessment: neither cited benchmark covers the late-2026 releases (Redis 8.2+ throughput or latency, Valkey 9.x). gaps.question: independent-benchmarks
gaps.reason: Checker's assessment: both cited benchmarks are synthetic single-node tests on one AWS Graviton4 instance type (c8g.2xl), run with Momento's own tuning and harness. Nothing covers cluster mode, persistence enabled, mixed GET/SET ratios or other hardware, and the throughput post itself warns that its results do not apply generally.
